Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{5\pi }{6}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}+(-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+144{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{16({cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta ))}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the arc length of the polar curve $r={4}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={4}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={4}^{\theta }\operatorname{ln}⁡4.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({4}^{\theta })}^{2}+{({4}^{\theta }\operatorname{ln}⁡4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{4}^{2\theta }+{4}^{2\theta }{ln}^{2}⁡4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(1+{ln}^{2}⁡4){4}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{1+{ln}^{2}⁡4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{4}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{1+{ln}^{2}⁡4}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\cdot {4}^{\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{ln}^{2}⁡4}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\cdot ({4}^{\pi /2}-{4}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{1+{ln}^{2}⁡4}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}({4}^{\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length $L$ of the polar curve $r=3+3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above). Do not round the answer.

*Hint: You may wish to use the following identity: $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}.$*

$L=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3+3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{(3+3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{9+18\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3i}\sqrt{18+18\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{18}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the identity for $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}):$

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}
$$

Therefore, using $x=\theta $ in the previous identity, the integral can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =3\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={6\cdot 2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =12(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =12(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}

questions.problem:
Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

*Hint: You may wish to use the following identity: $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the identity for $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2}):$

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}
$$

Therefore, using $x=\theta $ in the previous identity, the integral can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={2(-2)(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-4(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-1) \\  & =4-2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ is given by

$$
L =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=3-\sin(7\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} =-7\cos(7\theta)
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(3-\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta ))^{2}+(-7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+49{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+1+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{10-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14151533/assets/0bb9e5e7315d4bcd5fc21700fdd2597f6d9b585a109145de53c6f94e9530eabf.png)

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2(1-\cos\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ (shown in blue in the picture above).
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ is given by

$$
L =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=2(1-\cos\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 2\sin\theta.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now use the half-angle formula $1-\cos\theta =2\sin^2\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={-4\cdot 2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-8(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-8(0-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To calculate the arc length of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ between the rays $\theta=\theta_1$ and $\theta=\theta_2,$ we can use the formula

$$
L = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

For example, suppose that we want to find the arc length of the polar curve $r = 2,$ where $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{2\pi}{3}.$ The required arc length is shown in blue in the picture below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14151533/assets/e91cd717469db56426e39e8975aa04710ff2357c7a0d5de9d20f99bc5edcbb1c.png)

We will use the formula to compute the arc length. Since $r=2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 0,
$$

and therefore, the arc length can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{2\pi /3}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{2\pi /3}2\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /6}^{2\pi /3}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\theta \,{|}_{\pi /6}^{2\pi /3} \\  & =2(\frac{2\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Derivation of the Main Formula
tutorials.problem:
We've been using the following formula to compute the arc length bounded by a polar curve:

$$
L = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{ r^2 + \left( \frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} \right)^2} \:\textrm{d}\theta
$$

But where does this formula come from? Let's start with the familiar formula for the arc length of a parametric curve:

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left(\frac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 }\textrm{d}t
$$

A polar curve is really just a parametric curve with parameter $\theta$ and parametric equations given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the arc length formula for a parametric function with parameter $\theta,$ we have

$$
L = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{ \left(\frac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\textrm{d}\theta .
$$

Since $x = r \cos \theta,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, since $y=r\sin \theta,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our expression for $L,$ we reach the desired formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
